passage:
At the colony birthday party, all the children grabbed slices of chocolate cake. Tanuja, five, got a bowl of fruit and a small piece of the special cake Papa had brought.
She stared at the other plates. "Why can't I eat like them?"
Saurabh, her papa, knelt down. "Your body needs a bit of extra help, so the doctor helps us choose your food. It's nobody's fault. It's just how your body works."
Tanuja poked her fruit.
Then the balloon-popping game began. Tanuja burst four balloons before anyone else. "I'm the fastest popper!" she shouted.
"You are," Saurabh laughed.

qa.q: How many balloons did Tanuja burst?
qa.a: She burst four balloons before anyone else.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel when she saw the other plates?
qa.a: She felt left out and puzzled, which is why she asked why she couldn't eat like them.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that helped Tanuja?
qa.a: He gave a short, honest answer that it was nobody's fault and then cheered for what she was good at.

qa.q: If you were Saurabh, what would you want Tanuja to remember from the party?
qa.a: You would want her to remember feeling proud as the fastest popper, not only the different food.

grounding: It shows a young child with a long-term condition noticing she eats differently and asking why, and how an honest answer and pride protect her self-worth.

passage:
"Papa, why can everyone run and I can't?" Parveen asked, as her father, Tushar, lifted her into the car after the park.
"Your legs work differently from theirs. That's why you have your wheelchair. It helps you get around."
"But they were playing tag."
"You were sad you couldn't catch them?"
Parveen nodded. "A bit."
"That makes sense. But guess what I saw? I saw a girl catch the ball every time Rohit threw it. Even the tricky ones."
Parveen smiled. "I caught them all."
"You did. Tomorrow, a catching game?"
"And I'll win."
"Maybe!"

qa.q: What did Parveen catch every time?
qa.a: She caught the ball every time Rohit threw it.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel when the others played tag?
qa.a: She felt a bit sad and left out because she couldn't catch them.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that protected Parveen's self-worth?
qa.a: He gave a simple honest answer, named her sad feeling and then reminded her of her catching skill.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel hearing Parveen's question?
qa.a: He may feel a pang of sadness for her but wants to answer calmly and truthfully so she feels proud, not less.

grounding: It shows a young child with a disability noticing others can run and asking why, and a parent answering honestly and building pride in what she can do.

passage: At the temple fair in their village near Hubli, Avni, five, stood with her walker and watched her cousins race round the banyan tree. 'Amma, why can't my legs run like theirs?' Bhavna knelt beside her. 'Your legs work differently, kanna. The muscles need help, so you have your walker, like I need my glasses.' Avni frowned at the running children. 'I want to run.' 'I know.' Bhavna squeezed her hand. 'But guess who climbed all the temple steps by herself this morning?' Avni's face lifted. 'Me!' 'You. Every single step.' Avni straightened up. 'Let's go tell Ajji.'

qa.q: What did Avni use at the fair?
qa.a: Her walker.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling as she watched her cousins run?
qa.a: She felt sad and left out, wishing she could run like them.

qa.q: What made Bhavna's answer helpful?
qa.a: It was honest and simple, compared the walker to glasses, and then reminded Avni of something she was proud of.

qa.q: How might Ajji feel when Avni tells her about the steps?
qa.a: Ajji is likely to feel proud and delighted with her granddaughter.

grounding: Shows a young child with a disability noticing others running and asking why, and a parent giving an honest simple answer and pride in what she can do.

passage: At a friend's birthday party in Leeds, Bilal, six, watched the others grab cake. His mum, Priscila, was waiting with his blood-testing kit. 'Why do I always have to check first? Nobody else does.' Priscila crouched. 'Your body doesn't make enough of something called insulin, so the doctor helps us look after it.' Bilal kicked the table leg. 'It's not fair.' 'Sometimes it isn't.' She smiled. 'But who scored two goals at football yesterday? And who does his own finger check now, like a scientist?' Bilal grinned. 'Me.' He did the check himself, then had cake with everyone.

qa.q: What did Priscila have waiting at the party?
qa.a: His blood-testing kit.

qa.q: How did Bilal feel about checking before cake?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair and frustrating that nobody else had to do it.

qa.q: What did Priscila do that protected Bilal's self-worth?
qa.a: She explained simply and honestly, agreed it was unfair sometimes, and reminded him of things he was proud of.

qa.q: How might the other children see Bilal doing his own check?
qa.a: They might be curious and even impressed by him doing it like a scientist.

grounding: Shows a young child with a long-term illness noticing he is different and asking why, and a parent giving an honest simple answer and pride in his abilities.

passage: In the kindergarten, Yash, five, sat down after running in the garden and took two puffs from his inhaler, as he did most days. 'Why do you have that?' asked Maya. Yash looked at Urmila Teacher. 'Why do I, Miss? Nobody else does.' Urmila Teacher sat down beside them. 'Yash has asthma. Sometimes his breathing tubes get tight, and the puffer helps them open. Lots of people have it.' Maya nodded. Yash looked at the inhaler. 'I'm the only one.' 'In this class, yes. And you're the best in the class at knowing when your body needs help.' Yash sat taller. 'I do it all by myself.'

qa.q: What did Yash take after running?
qa.a: Two puffs from his inhaler.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when Maya asked about the inhaler?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a bit different, since nobody else in his class had one.

qa.q: What did Urmila Teacher do that protected Yash's self-worth?
qa.a: She gave a simple honest explanation and praised him for knowing when his body needed help.

qa.q: How might Maya see Yash's inhaler after the explanation?
qa.a: She probably sees it as ordinary and interesting rather than strange.

grounding: Shows a young child with a long-term condition noticing he is different and asking why, and a teacher giving a simple honest answer and pride in what he does.

passage:
Monday: At sports hour Imran watched the others race. At pickup he asked his papa, Jeevan, "Why are my legs slow?"
Wednesday: Jeevan sat with him on the steps. "Your legs grew differently, so they tire faster. Nobody did anything wrong." Imran thought, then asked, "Will they get fast?" "Not fast. But strong in their own way."
Saturday: At the park Imran balanced on the kerb longer than his cousin and shouted, "Papa, look! I'm the best balancer!" Jeevan clapped hard.

qa.q: What did Imran ask at pickup on Monday?
qa.a: He asked, "Why are my legs slow?"

qa.q: How was Imran feeling on Saturday at the park, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, shouting that he was the best balancer.

qa.q: What did Jeevan's answer on Wednesday get right?
qa.a: It was honest and simple, told Imran nobody was to blame, and pointed to his strength without promising what isn't true.

qa.q: How might Jeevan have felt hearing Imran's first question?
qa.a: Jeevan was probably a little sad and careful, wanting to answer truthfully without hurting Imran's pride.

grounding: Shows a young child with a disability noticing that others run faster and asking why, and an honest simple answer plus pride in what he can do protecting his self-worth.
